label: Minimal-shape cold start + hot path (default budget)
subject: samples/MinimalApp

notes.coldStartMs: Baseline 420 ms is the minimum of six Release boots of samples/MinimalApp on a QUIET 2026-09-12 dev machine (420/445/456/458/459/477). The same six boots on the SAME machine under load measured 1378/1461/1599/1645/2388/2564 - min 1378, over 3x the quiet minimum. That second run is why the ceiling is 6000 and not Phase 16's 2000: 2 s was measured once by hand on a deployment target and is a fine claim about a deployment, but as a CI ceiling on a shared runner it would flake, and a gate that flakes is a gate people disable. 6000 is ~14x the quiet baseline and ~4.4x the loaded one.
notes.hotPathMs: 5 ms against a 0.36 ms quiet baseline is deliberately ~14x slack; the loaded run measured min 0.688 ms (median 5.6 ms, which is why the gate reads min and not median). These ceilings exist to catch an ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE regression - a default path that starts doing I/O, a middleware registered unconditionally, a per-request allocation storm - not a percent-level one. Slack that has gone stale is not left to anyone's memory: every green run prints the measured headroom ratio, and ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests refuses a ceiling more than 20x its recorded baseline.
notes.statistic: Wallclock noise on a shared runner is one-sided - a neighbouring job can only make a boot slower - so the minimum over N runs is the least contaminated estimate, and the only statistic whose spread does not widen as the runner gets busier.
notes.absentAssemblies: The zero-cost-when-unused invariant (GP 13, and the Phase 9y 'default-on DROPPED' conclusion) made byte-level rather than timed. A companion nobody registered should not be in the deployment at all - which is checkable exactly, where 'costs no measurable time' is not.
notes.remotingDispatchColdStart: Recorded, not gated (Phase 906). Phase 804's ToolUp.Remoting.Benchmarks re-run after the generated invocation moved INSIDE the proxy: cold start of dispatching five methods of the sample's 40-method echo contract in a fresh process, min of 7 boots, Release, 16 logical cores, .NET 10.0.8, 2026-09-29, on a LOADED machine (other build-and-test sessions beside it). Generated table registered, dispatched through the proxy the adapter builds - the route a deployment takes, inside the pre-flight chain: 89.1 ms (standalone boots) / 109.8 ms (within the full report run). Reflective proxy, nothing registered: 107.7 / 122.7 ms; before the phase, the same arm on the same machine the same day measured 113.2 ms. Phase 804's direct floor - a typed call with no proxy and so no chain, which no deployment may use: 77.4 / 89.6 ms. So the safe route keeps roughly 13-18 ms (12-17 %) of the ~30 ms 804 measured for the bypass; per-request cost is level with reflection. Reproduce: dotnet build src/ToolUp.Remoting.Benchmarks -c Release, then dotnet src/ToolUp.Remoting.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net10.0/ToolUp.Remoting.Benchmarks.dll --boots 7 --rounds 9 (or --cold dispatch generated|reflection|direct for one boot).
notes.reviewing-a-change: Raising a ceiling is a claim that the SDK is now legitimately slower. Say why in this block, in the same diff.

client.label: Browser runtime under Node - boot, decode, dispatch-to-render (Phase 849); production bundle sizes (Phase 909)
client.subject: samples/MinimalClient (boot; its production build and the SDK shell's) + src/ToolUp.AI.Client.Tests ClientBench (decode over tests/remoting-corpus, dispatch over a 200-row view)

notes.remeasured: Phase 909 re-measured every clock below on Phase 884's tree, by the rule Phase 849 set them by (minimum over three production-build ClientBench runs, seed 849001, 6 boots, 9 rounds), because 884 found the seeded generator ClientBench orders its work by had overflowed under Fable - after a few draws every value was 0, so 849's baselines were taken over a near-degenerate decode order and dispatch sequence. Machine: Windows 11, Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 16 logical processors, node v25.9.0 win32/x64, 2026-09-29. Three runs on 884's own tree while six other build-and-test sessions shared the machine (CPU 51-72%): boot 617.0 / 622.5 / 603.7 ms, decode 3.921 / 2.523 / 1.648 us, view 375.3 / 358.6 / 392.6 us. The three runs the baselines are taken from are on the tree this phase shipped (884's plus the bundle and generated-module legs, which run in child processes and do not touch the in-process decode and view loops), at 9-14% CPU for two of them. Every ceiling moved down, because every baseline did; both numbers are in each note. The two causes cannot be separated after the fact: 849's runs were taken at a load average of 100%, and 884's fix changed the order the rounds walk.
notes.bootMs: Baseline 529.77 ms (was 1265): the minimum of three production-build runs, 529.77 / 536.08 / 534.79. Ceiling 7500 ms (was 17500), ~14x, Phase 192's slack ratio - the loaded runs on 884's tree (603.7 min) sit at 12x headroom under it. Boot is import() of the transpiled samples/MinimalClient to its first commit into #elmish-app under jsdom; import cost transfers to a browser, paint does not (jsdom lays nothing out and AG Charts draws into a no-op canvas).
notes.decodePerResponseUs: Baseline 1.545 us (was 5.66): the minimum of 1.559 / 1.588 / 1.545, the proxy's 200 path - SimpleJson.parseNative then Convert.fromJsonAs over createTypeInfo - averaged across the 72 cross-host wire-corpus .json fixtures that decode to their declared value (decimal-max and date-timespan-negative do not, and are excluded by name on every run). JSON.parse alone over the same bytes measured 0.236 us and parseNative alone 0.619 us in the same runs. Ceiling 22 us (was 80), ~14x. The loaded runs on 884's tree reached 3.921 us, 5.6x headroom under it. Decode is the same JavaScript a browser runs.
notes.viewPerDispatchUs: Baseline 315.29 us (was 906): the minimum of 385.08 / 371.78 / 315.29 of the view the render hook builds per dispatched message - a 200-row Feliz table, one render-hook call per message - with React's production build (the development build is refused by the harness, it validates every element). Ceiling 4400 us (was 12500), ~14x. View construction is the same JavaScript a browser runs; React's commit and paint are not in this number.
notes.minimalBundleKiB: Baseline 2663.43 KiB = 2,727,355 bytes: the one .js file `vite build` writes for samples/MinimalClient's index.html (790,119 bytes gzipped, a lever in the measurement file). Nearly all of it is the npm dependencies the sample's view pulls in (AG Grid, React); the sample never reaches the SDK shell, the remoting proxies or the generated client module, so this number moves with the sample's own reach and its dependency pins. A SIZE, not a clock: three builds from two separate Fable compiles wrote the same file byte for byte (same content hash in its name), so there is no noise for slack to absorb. The ceiling is therefore NOT the clocks' 14x: 2730 KiB, 1.025x, about 67 KiB of growth before a reviewed raise.
notes.shellBundleKiB: Baseline 3851.92 KiB = 3,944,367 bytes: `vite build --config vite.shell.config.mts` in samples/MinimalClient - the SDK shell's module graph (SDK.Client as the entry, every export kept), which holds the remoting proxies and the Phase 853 generated client module (1,058,664 bytes gzipped). Byte-identical across three builds, like the minimal bundle. Ceiling 3950 KiB, 1.025x: about 98 KiB of headroom, which is LESS than one more generated module the size of Phase 853's (its transpiled module minifies alone to 113,152 bytes), so the next one fails this gate instead of growing the bundle unseen. Measured on Windows; if the Linux runner's build differs by more than the headroom on its first run, re-take the baseline from that run's artefact and say so here - a platform difference is not a regression.
notes.bundle-headroom: Why the two sizes do not use the clocks' ~14x: that slack exists because wallclock noise on a shared runner is one-sided, and a size has none. ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests holds every shipped bundle ceiling to at most 1.1x its baseline, beside the 20x law every client ceiling is held to.
notes.statistic: Min over rounds (decode, view) and over fresh-process boots (boot), for Phase 192's reason: wallclock noise is one-sided.
notes.reproducing: pwsh ./dev-scripts/perf-budget-gate.ps1 -SkipServer -SkipLoad runs the whole client half: the two production builds into artifacts/perf-budget/bundles/, then, in src/ToolUp.AI.Client.Tests, NODE_ENV=production node --import ./register-loader.mjs output/Program.js ClientBench --seed 849001 --minimal-bundle <dir> --shell-bundle <dir>. The seed orders the fixtures and the dispatch sequence, and is printed beside the runtime on every run.
notes.reviewing-a-change: Raising a client ceiling is a claim that the client runtime is now legitimately slower, or its bundle legitimately larger. Say why here, in the same diff; ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests refuses any ceiling more than 20x its baseline, and any bundle ceiling more than 1.1x.

load.label: Fact and retrieval paths under concurrent load (Phase 886)
load.subject: src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks `load gate`: retrieval = flat store, memory blob arm, 10,000 chunks, 8 concurrent callers, 200 queries x 5 rounds; facts = BlobFactStore, memory blob arm, 1,000 subjects x 3 metrics x 4 weeks (12,000 facts), 4 concurrent callers, 20 operations x 5 rounds per operation

notes.remeasured: Phase 929 (2026-09-29) re-took the four fact figures Phase 890's point-read index changed (point read, assert, batch assert, reads per point read), as the minimum over three `load gate` runs on the same machine under the same kind of load: six build-and-test sessions beside it, CPU 94-99%, 8.8-13.9 GB free. The retrieval and population-read baselines are 886's: the three re-runs measured retrieval p95 41.50 / 37.42 / 40.49 ms and population read 17.93 / 23.90 / 17.61 ms, inside the spread of 886's own runs, so moving them would record noise.
notes.machine: Every baseline is the minimum over three `load gate` runs on 2026-09-28: Windows 11, Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 16 logical processors, 31.5 GB. It was NOT a quiet machine - six build-and-test sessions ran beside it, CPU load read 93% and 2.5 GB of memory was free - so, like the client block's baselines, these overstate the quiet cost. The per-run spread shows it: the population read's min-over-rounds p95 was 87.15 / 13.40 / 32.54 ms across the three runs.
notes.retrievalP95Ms: Baseline 32.38 ms (runs: 42.16 / 32.38 / 41.38). The value is the p95 of TOTAL retrieval latency within one round - measured around IRetrievalPipeline.Retrieve by RagTelemetry.RetrievalMeter, embedding, dense search, BM25, fusion and merge included - and the gate reads the minimum over five rounds. Ceiling ~14x (Phase 192's slack ratio).
notes.retrievalBlobReadsPerQuery: Baseline 0: once the scope's index is loaded (the warm-up pays it), the flat store and the BM25 index answer from memory and read no blob per query. The count is deterministic, so its ceiling is the baseline itself: a retrieval path that starts reading blobs per query has changed shape, whatever the clock says. On object storage each read is a request, which is why this is gated beside the clock rather than instead of it.
notes.factPointReadMs: Baseline 51.70 ms (Phase 929 re-measure, runs: 55.35 / 55.86 / 51.70; was 182.52 from 886's runs 297.36 / 182.52 / 268.20). A subject-and-metric read (FactQuery.forSubjectMetric, latest week). Phase 890's point-read index landed between 886's measurement and 929's, so the store no longer enumerates the scope per read, and the old ceiling (2500) sat 48x above what the path now costs - it could no longer see an order-of-magnitude regression. Ceiling 720, ~14x.
notes.factPopulationReadMs: Baseline 13.40 ms (runs: 87.15 / 13.40 / 32.54 - the widest spread in the block, and the reason its ceiling is ~13x of the quiet-est run rather than of the median). A top-10 population read over one metric's latest week; the scope is above the Phase 702 surface's 512-head threshold, so the surface is consulted (491 blob reads per read on average, cold builds included, against 12,000 for the enumerating point read). Ceiling ~13x.
notes.factAssertMs: Baseline 68.16 ms (Phase 929 re-measure, runs: 82.24 / 68.16 / 73.35; was 243.71). One Assert superseding the latest week of a distinct subject - since Phase 890 the lineage head is found through the point-read index (2 blob reads and 2 lists per assert, not the scope). Ceiling 950, ~14x.
notes.factBatchAssertMs: Baseline 94.13 ms (Phase 929 re-measure, runs: 99.48 / 104.85 / 94.13; was 233.38). One AssertBatch of 50 drafts, each superseding (51 blob reads per batch). Ceiling 1300, ~14x.
notes.factBlobReadsPerPointRead: Baseline 480.96 (Phase 929 re-measure; identical in all three runs; was 12,000 = the whole scope, before Phase 890's point-read index). Per read the index costs about one leaf plus the fact; the rest is the index the first reads of a fresh scope build, amortised over the 100 measured reads, so the figure depends on the cell and is deterministic for it. Ceiling 720, 1.5x: a point read that goes back to reading the scope (12,000) is 17x over it on any backend, whatever the clock says.
notes.statistic: Min over rounds, for Phase 192's reason: wallclock noise is one-sided. Each round is a closed loop of N concurrent callers; a round's value is the p95 of its own operations.
notes.largestMeasured: Recorded, not gated (Phase 929, carrying Phase 14k's deferred 500,000-chunk p95). The flat store at 500,000 chunks could not be held on the shared machine: stopped 172 s into its seed at a 7.56 GB working set with 2.3 GB of the machine free (CPU 97%, 12.1 GB free when it started). The largest size that ran is 250,000 chunks - p95 1,371.40 ms, p50 1,133.28 ms, 6.7 q/s at 8 callers, 40 queries x 3 rounds, about 6.5 GB of process memory (CPU 94%, 7.0 GB free at start). The flat scan's p95 is linear at about 5.5 us per chunk across 10,000 / 100,000 / 250,000, which puts 500,000 at ~2.75 s. Too large and too slow for a per-push gate; the 10,000-chunk cell above is what is gated. docs/rag/performance.md has the rows.
notes.reproducing: dotnet build src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks -c Release, then dotnet src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net10.0/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks.dll load gate --measurements artifacts/perf-budget/load-measurements.json. The full matrix (other stores, blob arms and sizes) is `load retrieval` / `load facts`; docs/rag/performance.md records what it measured.
notes.reviewing-a-change: Raising a load ceiling is a claim that the fact or retrieval path is now legitimately slower. Say why here, in the same diff; ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests refuses any ceiling more than 20x its baseline.

loadAzurite.label: Fact and retrieval paths under concurrent load - the object-storage arm (Phase 929)
loadAzurite.subject: src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks `load gate --arm azurite`: retrieval = the `load` block's cell with the blob arm on the Azure Blob companion over the local Azurite emulator; facts = BlobFactStore over the same emulator, 250 subjects x 3 metrics x 4 weeks (3,000 facts), 4 concurrent callers, 10 operations x 5 rounds per operation

notes.machine: Every baseline is the minimum over three `load gate --arm azurite` runs on 2026-09-29: Windows 11, Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 16 logical processors, 31.5 GB, Azurite (mcr.microsoft.com/azure-storage/azurite, blob service only) in Docker Desktop on the same machine. NOT a quiet machine: six build-and-test sessions ran beside it, CPU load read 88-100% and 9-14 GB was free. Each run took 114-148 s of wall time.
notes.arming: Not run by CI: the perf-budget job starts no emulator. Run it with `pwsh ./dev-scripts/perf-budget-gate.ps1 -SkipServer -SkipClient -LoadArms azurite` after `docker compose -f compose.parity.yml up -d --wait` and `$env:TOOLUP_PARITY_AZURITE = "UseDevelopmentStorage=true"`. An arm that is named but not armed fails; it never falls back to the memory arm.
notes.retrievalP95Ms: Baseline 28.35 ms (runs: 40.03 / 28.35 / 37.81) - the memory arm's figure within noise, because the flat store and the BM25 index answer from memory once the warm-up has loaded them; the emulator is paid in the seed and the warm-up, not per query. Ceiling 400, ~14x.
notes.retrievalBlobReadsPerQuery: Baseline 0, measured, as on the memory arm: no blob is read per query once warm. Deterministic, so the ceiling is the baseline.
notes.factPointReadMs: Baseline 1613.64 ms (runs: 1719.36 / 1613.64 / 1672.12). Every blob read is an HTTP request to the emulator, and a fresh scope's first point reads build the Phase 890 index over the whole scope (240.92 reads per read, amortised over the 50 measured reads) - so the clock is dominated by requests, which is what this arm exists to show. Ceiling 22000, ~13.6x.
notes.factPopulationReadMs: Baseline 741.11 ms (runs: 741.11 / 833.83 / 992.47). 310 blob reads per read on average, cold surface builds included. Ceiling 10000, ~13.5x.
notes.factAssertMs: Baseline 1793.30 ms (runs: 1952.48 / 1936.76 / 1793.30). Two blob reads and two prefix LISTS per assert; on the emulator the lists over the 3,000-blob scope are the cost - a list is a paged request of its own. Ceiling 25000, ~13.9x.
notes.factBatchAssertMs: Baseline 2450.52 ms (runs: 5772.83 / 2450.52 / 3092.75 - the widest spread in the block). 189 blob reads per batch of 50. Ceiling 34000, ~13.9x.
notes.factBlobReadsPerPointRead: Baseline 240.92, identical in all three runs: the index build amortised over 50 reads, plus about one leaf and the fact per read. Deterministic for the cell, so the ceiling is 1.5x, as on the memory arm.
notes.statistic: Min over rounds, for Phase 192's reason: wallclock noise is one-sided.
notes.reproducing: dotnet build src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks -c Release, then dotnet src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net10.0/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks.dll load gate --arm azurite --measurements artifacts/perf-budget/load-azurite-measurements.json, with TOOLUP_PARITY_AZURITE set.
notes.reviewing-a-change: Raising a ceiling is a claim that the path is now legitimately slower on object storage. Say why here, in the same diff; ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests refuses any ceiling more than 20x its baseline.

loadPostgres.label: Fact and retrieval paths under concurrent load - the database arm (Phase 929)
loadPostgres.subject: src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks `load gate --arm postgres`: retrieval = the `load` block's cell (10,000 chunks, 8 concurrent callers, 200 queries x 5 rounds) with the vector store on the pgvector companion (HNSW index, m=16, ef_construction=64); facts = the `load` block's fact cell - 1,000 subjects x 3 metrics x 4 weeks (12,000 facts), 4 concurrent callers, 20 operations x 5 rounds per operation - against the database-backed fact store (ToolUp.FactStores.Postgres, Phase 888), seeded through AssertBatch. Both over one local PostgreSQL 17, each in a table of its own per run, dropped afterwards.

notes.machine: Every baseline is the minimum over three `load gate --arm postgres` runs on 2026-09-29: Windows 11, Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 16 logical processors, 31.5 GB, PostgreSQL 17 (the pgvector/pgvector:pg17 image, default configuration) in Docker Desktop on the same machine. NOT a quiet machine: six build-and-test sessions ran beside it, CPU load read 94-100% (22% as the third run ended) and about 15 GB was free. Each run took 57-62 s of wall time, 47-54 s of it the pgvector seed (10,000 single-row upserts into an HNSW-indexed table).
notes.arming: Not run by CI: the perf-budget job starts no database. Run it with `pwsh ./dev-scripts/perf-budget-gate.ps1 -SkipServer -SkipClient -LoadArms postgres`, with TOOLUP_PGVECTOR_CONNECTION_STRING naming a local PostgreSQL - the same variable the pgvector arm reads, since one local server serves both; the fact store needs no extension. An arm that is named but not armed fails.
notes.retrievalP95Ms: Baseline 3.65 ms (runs: 3.81 / 4.03 / 3.65). The minimum over rounds hides a wide spread WITHIN each run: over all 1,000 queries the p50 was 51.24 / 49.84 / 3.59 ms and the p95 69.28 / 67.17 / 62.11 ms - the first rounds after the seed are an order of magnitude slower than the last, as the database settles the freshly built index. The gate reads the minimum, which is stable across runs. Ceiling 51, ~14x.
notes.retrievalBlobReadsPerQuery: Baseline 0, measured: the pgvector store keeps nothing in blobs and the BM25 index answers from memory once warm. Deterministic, so the ceiling is the baseline.
notes.factPointReadMs: Baseline 2.42 ms (runs: 2.56 / 2.77 / 2.42). One indexed query. Three earlier runs of the fact half alone, the first straight after the container started, read 8.96 / 3.56 / 3.51 ms. Ceiling 34, ~14x.
notes.factPopulationReadMs: Baseline 8.59 ms (runs: 12.94 / 10.13 / 8.59). The earlier fact-only runs read 138.86 / 20.68 / 11.72 ms, the first with the database's cache cold straight after the container started - 16x this baseline. So the ceiling is 170 (19.8x, inside the 20x law) rather than ~14x, which a first run on a fresh container would breach with no regression. It scales with the scope: at 300,000 facts the same read measured 296 ms (see docs/rag/performance.md).
notes.factAssertMs: Baseline 6.27 ms (runs: 6.57 / 7.36 / 6.27; the fact-only runs 12.02 / 15.74 / 10.02). One superseding assert: a head lookup and a write in one transaction. Ceiling 88, ~14x.
notes.factBatchAssertMs: Baseline 19.07 ms (runs: 19.84 / 19.86 / 19.07; the fact-only runs 40.09 / 30.27 / 23.42). One AssertBatch of 50 superseding drafts. Ceiling 267, ~14x.
notes.factBlobReadsPerPointRead: Baseline 0, measured: the database store reads no blob, so the harness's counter wraps a store nothing reads. The ceiling is the baseline - a database arm that starts reading blobs has changed shape.
notes.statistic: Min over rounds, for Phase 192's reason: wallclock noise is one-sided.
notes.reproducing: dotnet build src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks -c Release, then dotnet src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net10.0/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks.dll load gate --arm postgres --measurements artifacts/perf-budget/load-postgres-measurements.json, with TOOLUP_PGVECTOR_CONNECTION_STRING set.

loadPostgresHistory.label: The population read over a year of history - the database arm's large cell (Phase 962)
loadPostgresHistory.subject: src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks `load gate --arm postgres-history`: facts only - the database-backed fact store (ToolUp.FactStores.Postgres) over one local PostgreSQL, 2,500 subjects x 3 metrics x 52 weeks (390,000 facts, one metric's latest week = 1/156 of the table), seeded through AssertBatch into a table of its own and settled with VACUUM (ANALYZE), 4 concurrent callers, 20 operations x 5 rounds per operation; the row count from the population read's executed plan (PostgresFactStore.ExplainPopulation), taken once after the timed rounds.

notes.machine: Every baseline is the minimum over three `load gate --arm postgres-history` runs on 2026-10-01: Windows 11, Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 16 logical processors, 31.5 GB, PostgreSQL 17 (the pgvector/pgvector:pg17 image, default configuration) in Docker Desktop on the same machine, the container held to 6 GB. CPU load read 8-12% and 12-13 GB was free. Each run took 78-90 s of wall time, 74-85 s of it the seed.
notes.arming: Not run by CI: the perf-budget job starts no database. Run it with `pwsh ./dev-scripts/perf-budget-gate.ps1 -SkipServer -SkipClient -LoadArms postgres-history` (or beside the other arms: -LoadArms postgres,postgres-history), with TOOLUP_PGVECTOR_CONNECTION_STRING naming a local PostgreSQL. An arm that is named but not armed fails.
notes.why-this-cell: The `loadPostgres` block's fact cell carries 4 weeks, so a population read that stopped using the population index would scan a table only four times its population and could hide inside that block's clock ceiling. This cell carries 52 weeks over 3 metrics, so the same regression scans 156 times the population. The stated scale (300,000 x 3 x 52 = 46,800,000 facts) does not seed in a gate run: at about 4,000 facts a second it is over three hours. docs/rag/performance.md records the read measured at 10,000 to 100,000 subjects at this depth, and 300,000 at 4 weeks.
notes.factPopulationReadMs: Baseline 6.95 ms (runs: 6.95 / 7.17 / 7.53), the p95 of one round, min over rounds: an index-only scan of one metric's latest week, 2,500 heads. The same cell on the schema before Phase 962 (pop_idx, a parallel scan of the table) read 147.49 / 134.46 / 139.41 ms, about 20x. Ceiling 97, ~14x: it catches that regression, but only by about 1.4x. The row count below is the decisive guard; this clock is the backstop for a regression the count cannot see (an index-only scan that turned into heap fetches touches the same rows).
notes.factPopulationRowsPerRead: Baseline 2500, identical in all three runs: the table rows the population read's summary touched, from its executed plan. The read is an index-only scan of the asked week's heads, so the count is the population, one row per subject. It is deterministic for the cell, so the ceiling is 1.5x (3750), as for the blob-read counts. A read that falls back to the old schema's table scan touches 390,000 (156x). One that ranges over the metric's history, as an index keyed by period START does, touches 130,000 (52x).
notes.factAssertMs: Baseline 49.34 ms (runs: 49.34 / 49.66 / 49.77). One superseding assert. On this database it is dominated by the commit's flush, about 48 ms whatever the indexes: the old schema read 48.18 / 48.73 / 49.05. Budgeted here because the covering index is one more index insert per write, and this is the cell where the table is deep. Ceiling 690, ~14x.
notes.factBatchAssertMs: Baseline 56.49 ms (runs: 56.49 / 56.82 / 56.68; the old schema read 55.11 / 56.95 / 56.80). One AssertBatch of 50 superseding drafts. Ceiling 790, ~14x.
notes.flat-scale: Phase 940's deferred task asked for a flat-scale check if the read became flat. It is not flat across subject counts: it stays linear in the population (about 1.2 us per subject at the median, four callers, 10,000 to 100,000 subjects), because every statistic is defined over the selected population. What Phase 962 made flat is the cost across HISTORY - the same population costs the same with 4 weeks or 52 behind it - and the row count above is that check: it stays at the population whatever the depth.
notes.statistic: Min over rounds, for Phase 192's reason: wallclock noise is one-sided. The row count is one plan's count, the same in every round.
notes.reproducing: dotnet build src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks -c Release, then dotnet src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net10.0/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks.dll load gate --arm postgres-history --measurements artifacts/perf-budget/load-postgres-history-measurements.json, with TOOLUP_PGVECTOR_CONNECTION_STRING set.
notes.reviewing-a-change: Raising the population read's ceiling is a claim that the read is now legitimately slower; raising the row count's is a claim that it must now touch more than the asked population. Say why here, in the same diff; ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests refuses any ceiling more than 20x its baseline.
